> Before diving into this vignette, we recommend reading the vignettes [**Introduction to LaMa**](https://janolefi.github.io/LaMa/articles/Intro_to_LaMa.html) and [**Finer control**](https://janolefi.github.io/LaMa/articles/Finer_control.html).

```{r setup}
library(LaMa)
```

In standard HMMs, observations are assumed to arrive at **regular, equidistant time points**, so that the transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ can be given a consistent interpretation with respect to a fixed time unit (e.g. one hour or one day). In many real-world applications this assumption breaks down: animal telemetry fixes arrive at varying intervals, patient measurements are taken at unequal times, or data simply have gaps. Using a regular HMM in such cases leads to a misspecified transition structure, because the same $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is applied regardless of whether the time gap is short or long.

The natural remedy is to replace the discrete-time Markov chain with a **continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC)**. This vignette covers two cases:

- **Uninformative observation times**: the times are fixed or unrelated to the state process, and only the observed values carry information about the states. This leads to **continuous-time HMMs**.
- **Informative observation times**: the times are themselves generated by the state process, as for events that occur at a state-dependent rate. This leads to **Markov-modulated (marked) Poisson processes**.

## The generator matrix

A CTMC is fully characterised by its **(infinitesimal) generator matrix**
$$
\boldsymbol{Q} = \begin{pmatrix}
  -q_1 & q_{12} & \cdots & q_{1N} \\
  q_{21} & -q_2 & \cdots & q_{2N} \\
  \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
  q_{N1} & q_{N2} & \cdots & -q_N \\
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $q_{ij} \geq 0$ for $i \neq j$ and $q_i = \sum_{j \neq i} q_{ij}$, so that every row sums to zero.

The off-diagonal entry $q_{ij}$ is the **instantaneous rate** at which the process transitions from state $i$ to state $j$. Their sum $q_i$ is the total leaving rate from state $i$, and the **dwell time** (time spent in state $i$ before leaving) is exponentially distributed with rate $q_i$, i.e. with mean $1/q_i$. Conditional on leaving state $i$, the probability of moving to state $j \neq i$ is
$$
\omega_{ij} = \frac{q_{ij}}{q_i}.
$$
These two properties — the dwell time distribution and the conditional next-state probabilities — together fully describe the dynamics of the chain.

Throughout this vignette, we use the 3-state generator below. The mean dwell times are $1/0.5 = 2$, $1/2 = 0.5$ and $1/1 = 1$ time units, so state 1 is the most persistent state.

```{r generator}
Q = matrix(c(-0.5, 0.2, 0.3,
              1.0, -2.0, 1.0,
              0.4,  0.6, -1.0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
```

## From the generator to transition probabilities

Given $\boldsymbol{Q}$ and a time interval of length $\Delta t$, the transition probability matrix is obtained via the **matrix exponential**:
$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t) = \exp(\boldsymbol{Q} \, \Delta t).
$$
This follows from the Kolmogorov forward equations; see @dobrow2016introduction for details. The key practical point is that $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t)$ automatically adapts to the length of the interval: short gaps produce a matrix close to the identity (little chance of switching), and long gaps produce a matrix close to the stationary distribution (the process has had time to mix). `LaMa` computes this efficiently for an entire vector of time differences using `tpm_ct()`:

```{r tpm_ct_demo}
Gammas = tpm_ct(Q, c(0.1, 10)) # one matrix per time difference
round(Gammas[,,1], 3) # short gap: close to the identity
round(Gammas[,,2], 3) # long gap: each row close to the stationary distribution
stationary_ct(Q)
```


## Uninformative observation times: continuous-time HMMs

A **continuous-time HMM** combines the CTMC with a state-dependent observation process, observed at irregular times that carry no information about the states. One important prerequisite is the **snapshot property**: the observed value at time $t$ may only depend on the state *at that instant*, not on the history of the process or on how much time has elapsed since the previous observation. This is a reasonable assumption for many biological and physical processes. For more details see @glennie2023hidden.

### Likelihood

The likelihood of a continuous-time HMM for observations $x_{t_1}, \dots, x_{t_T}$ at irregular times $t_1 < \dots < t_T$ has **exactly the same structure** as the regular HMM likelihood:
$$
L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)} \boldsymbol{P}(x_{t_1})\, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t_1)\, \boldsymbol{P}(x_{t_2})\, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t_2)\, \boldsymbol{P}(x_{t_3}) \cdots \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t_{T-1})\, \boldsymbol{P}(x_{t_T})\, \boldsymbol{1}^\top,
$$
where $\Delta t_k = t_{k+1} - t_k$ and each $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t_k) = \exp(\boldsymbol{Q} \,\Delta t_k)$ is specific to its interval. The initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)}$ is typically set to the stationary distribution of the CTMC, available via `stationary_ct()`. Everything else — the allprobs matrix and the forward algorithm via `forward()` — is identical to the regular HMM case.

### Writing the negative log-likelihood function

The likelihood function follows the same pattern as a regular inhomogeneous HMM. The only addition is the `generator()` and `tpm_ct()` calls: `generator()` maps the unconstrained `log_qs` vector (one entry per off-diagonal element of $\boldsymbol{Q}$, on the log scale to ensure positivity) to a valid generator matrix, and `tpm_ct()` computes $\exp(\boldsymbol{Q} \, \Delta t)$ for every observed time difference at once. For the initial distribution, `stationary_ct()` computes the stationary distribution directly from $\boldsymbol{Q}$. `forward()` itself never sees $\boldsymbol{Q}$, only the matrices $\exp(\boldsymbol{Q} \, \Delta t)$. With `delta = "stationary"`, it would compute the stationary distribution of the first of these, which gives the same result, as $\exp(\boldsymbol{Q} \, \Delta t)$ has the same stationary distribution as $\boldsymbol{Q}$ for any $\Delta t > 0$.

```{r nll}
nll = function(par) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  mu = exp(log_mu); REPORT(mu)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma); REPORT(sigma)
  Q = generator(log_qs); REPORT(Q) # maps unconstrained params -> valid Q
  delta = stationary_ct(Q)         # stationary distribution of the CTMC
  Qube = tpm_ct(Q, timediff)       # exp(Q * dt) for each time difference
  allprobs = statedens(x, dnorm, mu, sigma)
  -forward(delta, Qube, allprobs)
}
```

### Simulating data

We first draw the observation times as a Poisson process with rate $1$, i.e. with exponentially distributed time differences. This represents an irregular but otherwise uninformative observation mechanism that is **not part of the model**. Given these times, we simulate states and observations from the model with the same likelihood function: we build the AD object at the true parameters with an all-`NA` placeholder for `x`, and `simulate()` draws each state from the row of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\Delta t)$ belonging to the previous state, and each observation given its state (see the vignette [**Longitudinal data**](https://janolefi.github.io/LaMa/articles/Longitudinal_data.html) for details). `generator()` fills the off-diagonal entries of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ by column, so `Q[row(Q) != col(Q)]` gives them in the right order.

```{r data}
mu = c(5, 15, 30) # state-dependent means
sigma = c(2, 3, 5) # state-dependent standard deviations

set.seed(123)
n = 500
obs_times = cumsum(rexp(n, 1)) # irregular observation times

par_true = list(
  log_mu = log(mu),
  log_sigma = log(sigma),
  log_qs = log(Q[row(Q) != col(Q)]) # off-diagonal entries of Q
)
dat = list(
  x = rep(NA, n), # placeholder for the observations
  timediff = diff(obs_times)
)

sim = simulate(lama(MakeADFun(nll, par_true, silent = TRUE)), seed = 123)
dat$x = sim$x
```

The plot below shows the first 50 observations, coloured by their true (latent) state, illustrating the irregular observation times.

```{r vis_ctHMM}
color = LaMaColors(3)

plot(obs_times[1:50], sim$x[1:50], pch = 16, bty = "n", col = color[sim$state[1:50]],
     xlab = "observation times", ylab = "x")
legend("topright", pch = 16, col = color, legend = paste("state", 1:3), box.lwd = 0)
```

### Fitting the model

A 3-state model has $N(N-1) = 6$ off-diagonal entries in $\boldsymbol{Q}$.

```{r model, warning = FALSE}
par = list(
  log_mu = log(c(5, 10, 25)),   # initial state-dependent means
  log_sigma = log(c(2, 2, 6)),  # initial state-dependent sds
  log_qs = rep(0, 6)            # initial off-diagonal generator entries (exp(0) = 1)
)

obj = MakeADFun(nll, par, silent = TRUE)
system.time(
  opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
)
mod = lama(obj)
```

### Results

```{r results}
mod$mu     # true: 5, 15, 30
mod$sigma  # true: 2, 3, 5
round(mod$Q, 3) # true: Q as defined above
```

The estimated generator can be interpreted directly: the mean dwell time in each state is $1/\hat{q}_i$.

```{r dwell_times}
round(1 / diag(-mod$Q), 2) # estimated mean dwell times; true: 2, 0.5, 1
```

The transition probability curves show how quickly the process mixes as the time difference grows. At $\Delta t = 0$, the probability $\gamma_{ii}(\Delta t)$ of being in state $i$ again after $\Delta t$ is one; as $\Delta t \to \infty$ it converges to the stationary probability of state $i$ (dashed lines), reflecting full mixing.

```{r tpm_curves}
dt_seq = seq(0, 10, length.out = 300)
Qube_seq = tpm_ct(mod$Q, dt_seq)
delta = stationary_ct(mod$Q)

plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 1), bty = "n",
     xlab = expression(Delta*t), ylab = expression(gamma[ii](Delta*t)))
for(i in 1:3) {
  lines(dt_seq, Qube_seq[i, i, ], lwd = 2, col = color[i])
  abline(h = delta[i], lty = 2, col = color[i]) # long-run limit
}
legend("topright", lwd = 2, col = color, legend = paste("state", 1:3), bty = "n")
```

We can also decode the most probable hidden state sequence using `viterbi()`. Because `forward()` automatically reports the initial distribution, the transition probability matrices and `allprobs`, we can pass the model object directly. As the data are simulated, we can compare the decoded states with the true ones.

```{r state_decoding}
states = viterbi(mod)
mean(states == sim$state) # proportion of correctly decoded states
```


## Informative observation times: Markov-modulated Poisson processes

In a continuous-time HMM, the observation *values* carry information about the latent state, while the observation *times* are uninformative. The **Markov-modulated Poisson process (MMPP)** reverses this: the **arrival times themselves are the observations**, and their spacing carries information about the hidden state process.

The CTMC modulates the rate of a Poisson process: while the chain stays in state $j$, events arrive at a constant, state-specific rate $\lambda_j$. A high-rate state produces rapid bursts of closely spaced arrivals; a low-rate state produces sparse events. The **Markov-modulated marked Poisson process (MMMPP)** additionally associates a random **mark** $y_i$ with each arrival, drawn from a state-dependent distribution at the moment of arrival, providing a second source of information about the latent state alongside the timing. For more background see @meier1987fitting and @langrock2013markov.

### Likelihood

For $n$ arrivals at times $t_1 < \dots < t_n$, let $\Delta t_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$ be the inter-arrival waiting times and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)$ the diagonal matrix of state-dependent rates. The likelihood of a stationary MMMPP is
$$
L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \boldsymbol{\pi}\,\boldsymbol{P}(y_1) \Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \exp\bigl((\boldsymbol{Q} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda})\,\Delta t_i\bigr)\,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\,\boldsymbol{P}(y_{i+1})\Bigr)\,\boldsymbol{1}^\top,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ is the stationary distribution of the CTMC and $\boldsymbol{P}(y_i)$ is a diagonal matrix of state-dependent densities evaluated at mark $y_i$. The matrix $\exp((\boldsymbol{Q} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda})\,\Delta t_i)$ propagates the state distribution through gap $\Delta t_i$ while accounting for the fact that *no* event occurred during this interval; $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ then contributes the instantaneous rate of the event that *does* occur at the end of the gap. Without marks (MMPP), the matrices $\boldsymbol{P}(y_i)$ are simply dropped.

This has **exactly the same structure** as the regular HMM likelihood, so `forward()` applies directly. `tpm_ct(Q, timediff, lambda)` computes the matrices $\exp((\boldsymbol{Q} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda})\,\Delta t_i)$, and we fold $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ into the `allprobs` matrix: after computing the mark densities for all $n$ arrivals, rows $2, \dots, n$ are multiplied by $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)$. For an MMPP, `allprobs` would hence have a first row of ones and all other rows equal to $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)$.

### Writing the negative log-likelihood function

Unlike for the continuous-time HMM, `forward("stationary", ...)` would be wrong here: the matrices $\exp((\boldsymbol{Q} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda})\,\Delta t_i)$ are not transition probability matrices (their rows sum to less than one), so their "stationary distribution" is not the one of the CTMC. The stationary distribution has to come from $\boldsymbol{Q}$ via `stationary_ct()`.

```{r nll2}
nll2 = function(par) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  lambda = exp(log_lambda); REPORT(lambda)
  REPORT(mu)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma); REPORT(sigma)
  Q = generator(log_qs); REPORT(Q)
  delta = stationary_ct(Q)
  Qube = tpm_ct(Q, timediff, lambda) # exp((Q - Lambda) * dt)
  allprobs = statedens(marks, dnorm, mu, sigma)
  # multiply rows 2:n by lambda to fold in the arrival-rate contribution
  allprobs[-1, ] = allprobs[-1, ] * rep(lambda, each = length(timediff))
  -forward(delta, Qube, allprobs)
}
```

### Simulating data

As the arrival times are now part of the data, we simulate them directly: we draw the sequence of states using the conditional next-state probabilities $\omega_{ij}$ and the exponential dwell times, and then within each sojourn of length `dwell` a Poisson number of arrivals with mean `lambda * dwell`, uniformly distributed over the sojourn. Each arrival gets a mark from the distribution of its state.

```{r simulation2}
lambda = c(1, 5, 20) # state-dependent arrival rates
mu = c(-5, 0, 5)     # state-dependent mark means
sigma = c(2, 1, 2)   # state-dependent mark sds

set.seed(123)
k = 200 # number of sojourns
s = numeric(k)
s[1] = sample(1:3, 1, prob = stationary_ct(Q))
for(t in 2:k) {
  omega = Q[s[t-1], ] / -Q[s[t-1], s[t-1]] # conditional next-state probabilities
  omega[s[t-1]] = 0
  s[t] = sample(1:3, 1, prob = omega)
}
dwell = rexp(k, -diag(Q)[s]) # dwell times
end = cumsum(dwell)          # end of each sojourn

# Poisson arrivals, uniformly distributed within each sojourn
n_arr = rpois(k, lambda[s] * dwell)
arrival_times = unlist(lapply(1:k, function(t) sort(runif(n_arr[t], end[t] - dwell[t], end[t]))))
state = rep(s, n_arr) # true state at each arrival
marks = rnorm(length(arrival_times), mu[state], sigma[state])
```

In the **cumulative arrivals plot**, the slope of the curve equals the current arrival rate, so steep segments correspond to the bursty state 3 and shallow segments to state 1. The marks additionally separate the states.

```{r vis_MMMPP, fig.dim = c(8, 4), fig.show = "hold"}
plot(arrival_times[1:300], 1:300, pch = 20, bty = "n", col = color[state[1:300]],
     xlab = "time", ylab = "cumulative arrivals")
legend("topleft", pch = 20, col = color, legend = paste("state", 1:3), box.lwd = 0)

plot(arrival_times[1:300], marks[1:300], pch = 16, bty = "n", col = color[state[1:300]],
     xlab = "time", ylab = "marks")
```

### Fitting the model

```{r model2, warning = FALSE}
par = list(
  log_lambda = log(c(2, 4, 15)), # initial arrival rates
  mu = c(-4, 0, 4),              # initial mark means
  log_sigma = log(c(1, 1, 1)),   # initial mark sds
  log_qs = rep(log(0.5), 6)      # initial off-diagonal generator entries
)
dat = list(
  marks = marks,
  timediff = diff(arrival_times)
)

obj2 = MakeADFun(nll2, par, silent = TRUE)
system.time(
  opt2 <- nlminb(obj2$par, obj2$fn, obj2$gr)
)
mod2 = lama(obj2)
```

### Results

```{r results2}
mod2$lambda                 # true: 1, 5, 20
mod2$mu                     # true: -5, 0, 5
mod2$sigma                  # true: 2, 1, 2
round(mod2$Q, 3)            # true: Q as defined above
round(1 / diag(-mod2$Q), 2) # mean dwell times; true: 2, 0.5, 1
```

Overlaying the fitted state-dependent densities on a histogram of all marks provides an intuitive model check. Note that the mixture weights are **not** the stationary distribution $\pi_j$ (proportion of *time* in state $j$) but the rate-weighted proportions $w_j \propto \pi_j \lambda_j$ -- states with higher arrival rates contribute disproportionately more marks.

```{r mark_density}
pi = stationary_ct(mod2$Q)
w = pi * mod2$lambda / sum(pi * mod2$lambda) # proportion of marks from each state

hist(marks, prob = TRUE, breaks = 50, border = "white", main = "", xlab = "mark")
for (j in 1:3) {
  curve(w[j] * dnorm(x, mod2$mu[j], mod2$sigma[j]),
        add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = color[j], n = 300)
}
curve(rowSums(sapply(1:3, function(j) w[j] * dnorm(x, mod2$mu[j], mod2$sigma[j]))),
      add = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2, n = 300)
legend("topright", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), bty = "n",
       col = c(color, "black"), legend = c(paste("state", 1:3), "marginal"))
```

State decoding via `viterbi()` combines both timing and mark information to assign the latent state:

```{r state_decoding2}
states2 = viterbi(mod2)
mean(states2 == state) # proportion of correctly decoded states
```
